title: Error Budgets
summary: Turning an SLO into a spendable budget that governs release velocity — the mechanism that turns reliability from an opinion into a policy.

slides.markdown:
An **error budget** is 100% minus your SLO — the amount of unreliability you're allowed to spend before reliability work must take priority over new features.

- It reframes reliability as a **resource** you spend, not a virtue you maximize.
- **Burn rate** — how fast you're consuming it — matters more than the raw remaining number.
- A budget without a **policy** for what happens when it hits zero is just a dashboard, not a control.

slides.subTitle: 100% minus the SLO, as a spendable allowance
slides.markdown:
If your SLO is 99.9% over 30 days, your **error budget** is the remaining 0.1% — about **43 minutes** of allowed downtime or failed requests that month. Every failed request, every risky deploy, every dependency blip **spends** from that same pool.

The reframe this enables: reliability stops being an unbounded goal ("more is always better") and becomes a **budget** — you can spend it on velocity (shipping fast, taking risks) as long as you don't overspend it.

slides.subTitle: How fast you're spending, not just how much is left
slides.markdown:
**Burn rate** measures how quickly you're consuming the error budget relative to a sustainable pace. A burn rate of **1x** means you'll exhaust the whole month's budget exactly at the end of the window — sustainable. A burn rate of **10x** means you'll exhaust a month's budget in about **3 days** if it continues.

Burn rate matters more than the raw number remaining: 95% of budget left sounds safe, but if you're burning it at 20x, you'll be at zero within hours — the number alone hides the trajectory.

| | Fast-burn alert | Slow-burn alert |
|---|---|---|
| Detects | A sudden, severe outage | A gradual, low-level degradation |
| Window | Short (e.g. 5–60 min) | Long (e.g. 6–24 hours) |
| Threshold | High burn rate (e.g. 14x) | Lower burn rate (e.g. 2–3x) |
| Urgency | Page immediately | Ticket or lower-urgency page |

Both alert on the *same* underlying budget, at different rates and time windows — you need both, or you'll either miss a slow leak or drown in pages for one bad minute.

slides.subTitle: What happens when it's exhausted
slides.markdown:
An error budget only has teeth if there's a **written policy** for what happens at zero. A typical policy: when the budget for a service is exhausted, **feature launches freeze** for that service until reliability work brings it back into the green — no exceptions for "just one more launch."

The policy is what makes the budget a genuine trade-off mechanism between product and engineering, rather than a metric that gets quietly ignored under launch pressure.

Error budgets exist to resolve a structural tension: product wants to **ship fast**, and unmanaged, ops wants to **never break anything** — left unresolved, that's just a permanent argument. The budget converts it into a shared, objective number both sides agree to in advance.

As long as budget remains, teams can take real risks — aggressive rollouts, experimental features. Once it's spent, the incentive flips automatically toward hardening, without anyone needing to "win" the argument in the moment.

slides.subTitle: A bad week freezes launches
slides.markdown:
A payments service has a 99.95% SLO (about 22 minutes/month of budget). A botched config push causes an 18-minute outage on Monday. By Wednesday, a flaky dependency adds another 6 minutes of errors — the month's budget is now spent, with three weeks still to go.

Per policy, the team **freezes new feature launches** for that service and reallocates the sprint to reliability: fixing the config validation gap and adding a circuit breaker for the flaky dependency — until the budget resets and trust is rebuilt.
